title: Phase Velocity in Waves
short_intro: Phase velocity is the rate at which the phase of a wave propagates in space. It represents the velocity at which a point of constant phase (such as a crest or trough) travels along the wave.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of phase velocity, relation between wave velocity, frequency, and wavelength, and simple numerical problems involving sinusoidal wave equations.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of phase velocity from the wave equation, relation between phase velocity and group velocity, dispersion relations, and dispersive media.

prerequisites: Simple harmonic motion and wave equation
Angular frequency, wave number, and wavelength

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Meaning
bullets: Phase velocity (v<sub>p</sub>) is defined as v<sub>p</sub> = ω/k, where ω is the angular frequency and k is the angular wave number.
It characterizes the propagation speed of a single frequency component (monochromatic wave) through a medium.
In a non-dispersive medium, all frequency components travel at the same phase velocity.

concept_notes.heading: Relation with Frequency and Wavelength
bullets: Expressing ω = 2πν and k = 2π/λ, the phase velocity is given by v<sub>p</sub> = νλ.
Here, ν is the frequency of the wave and λ is its spatial wavelength.
Any change in medium properties that alters λ while keeping ν constant will change the phase velocity.

concept_notes.heading: Dispersive vs Non-Dispersive Media
bullets: In a non-dispersive medium, phase velocity is independent of frequency or wavelength.
In a dispersive medium, the phase velocity depends on wavelength (dv<sub>p</sub>/dλ ≠ 0), leading to wave packet spreading.
Examples of dispersive media include deep water gravity waves and light passing through glass prisms.

concept_notes.heading: Relation to Group Velocity
bullets: Group velocity v<sub>g</sub> represents the velocity of the overall wave packet or envelope energy transport.
The fundamental relation linking them is v<sub>g</sub> = v<sub>p</sub> - λ(dv<sub>p</sub>/dλ).
In a normal dispersion medium, phase velocity is greater than group velocity (v<sub>p</sub> > v<sub>g</sub>).

derivations.title: Derivation of Phase Velocity from Wave Equation
steps: Consider a one-dimensional traveling harmonic wave represented by y(x, t) = A cos(kx - ωt + φ).
For a point of constant phase along the wave profile, the phase term must remain constant: kx - ωt = constant.
Differentiate both sides with respect to time t: k(dx/dt) - ω = 0.
Recognize dx/dt as the phase velocity v<sub>p</sub>, giving v<sub>p</sub> = ω/k.

derivations.title: Relation between Phase Velocity and Group Velocity
derivations.conditions: Dispersive medium where ω is a non-linear function of k
steps: Define group velocity as v<sub>g</sub> = dω/dk.
Express angular frequency in terms of phase velocity: ω = k v<sub>p</sub>.
Differentiate ω with respect to k using the product rule: v<sub>g</sub> = \frac{d}{dk}(k v<sub>p</sub>) = v<sub>p</sub> + k \frac{dv_p}{dk}.

Substitute k = 2π/λ and use chain rule \frac{dv_p}{dk} = \frac{dv_p}{d\lambda} \frac{d\lambda}{dk} = -\frac{\lambda}{2\pi} \lambda^2 \frac{dv_p}{d\lambda} to obtain v<sub>g</sub> = v<sub>p</sub> - λ\frac{dv_p}{d\lambda}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Wave Propagation Snapshot
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Displacement y versus position x at two successive times t and t + Δt, showing the forward shift of a wave crest.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The spatial displacement of the crest divided by Δt directly illustrates the phase velocity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in conceptual multiple-choice questions identifying crest travel speed.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Dispersion Relation Curve (ω vs k)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of angular frequency ω on the y-axis against wave number k on the x-axis. A straight line passing through the origin represents non-dispersive waves (v<sub>p</sub> = v<sub>g</sub>), while a curved plot represents dispersive waves.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the secant line from the origin gives the phase velocity (v<sub>p</sub> = ω/k), and the local tangent slope gives the group velocity (v<sub>g} = dω/dk).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in PGT to evaluate understanding of dispersive characteristics.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Kundt's Tube Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Experimental setup showing a horizontal glass tube with lycopodium powder, a vibrating piston at one end, and a fixed reflecting boundary.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Forms standing waves where the distance between consecutive heaps of powder equals half the wavelength (λ/2), allowing experimental determination of phase velocity v = νλ.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested as a classical acoustic experiment to measure wave speed in gases and solids.

solved_numericals.question: A progressive wave is represented by the equation y(x, t) = 0.05 sin(100πt - 2πx), where x is in meters and t is in seconds. Calculate the phase velocity of the wave.
solution_steps: Compare the given equation with the standard wave equation y(x, t) = A sin(ωt - kx).
Identify angular frequency ω = 100π rad s<sup>-1</sup> and wave number k = 2π rad m<sup>-1</sup>.

solved_numericals.question: Find the frequency of a wave whose phase velocity is 330 m s^-1 and wavelength is 1.5 m.
solution_steps: Use the relation between phase velocity, frequency, and wavelength: v<sub>p</sub> = νλ.
Rearrange to solve for frequency: ν = v<sub>p</sub> / λ.

solved_numericals.question: In a dispersive medium, the phase velocity is given by v<sub>p</sub> = a + bλ, where a and b are constants. Derive an expression for the group velocity v<sub>g</sub> in terms of a, b, and λ.
solution_steps: Start with the general relation between group velocity and phase velocity: v<sub>g</sub> = v<sub>p</sub> - λ(dv<sub>p</sub>/dλ).
Differentiate the given phase velocity expression with respect to λ: dv<sub>p</sub>/dλ = d/dλ(a + bλ) = b.
Substitute v<sub>p</sub> and dv<sub>p</sub>/dλ into the group velocity formula: v<sub>g</sub> = (a + bλ) - λ(b).
Simplify the expression: v<sub>g</sub> = a + bλ - bλ = a.

assumptions_and_limitations: Phase velocity applies strictly to monochromatic, single-frequency continuous waves and cannot directly represent the propagation speed of information or signal energy in dispersive media.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Phase velocity can always exceed the speed of light in vacuum without physical restriction.
common_misconceptions.correct: While phase velocity (v<sub>p</sub> = ω/k) can exceed c in certain anomalous dispersion regions or wave guides, it transmits no energy or information, thus not violating relativity.
common_misconceptions.why: Information and energy travel at the group velocity or signal velocity, which never exceeds c.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Phase velocity and group velocity are always identical.
common_misconceptions.correct: They are identical only in non-dispersive media where phase velocity is independent of frequency.
common_misconceptions.why: In dispersive media, different frequency components travel at different speeds, making v<sub>p</sub> different from v<sub>g</sub>.

quick_revision: Phase velocity is given by v_p = \omega/k = \nu\lambda and represents the speed of constant phase points.
